A good Philadelphia web designer has to understand two things about how this city does business. First, people shop by the corridor: East Passyunk, Germantown Avenue, Main Street in Manayunk, the blocks of Fishtown and Northern Liberties. Second, the city runs on paperwork, and customers increasingly check it. Every business here needs a Commercial Activity License, contractors carry license numbers the city expects to see on their advertising, and the storefront itself may have been fixed up with city money. A site that shows where you sit on your corridor and which licenses you hold answers questions most competitors leave open.

Dominion Web Design Pro writes those sites by hand. You see a free demo before you pay, and the price is printed: $497, $997 or $1,997, one time.

A city of about 1.57 million that shops street by street

The Census Bureau put Philadelphia at 1,574,281 residents in July 2025. Those residents do much of their everyday buying on neighborhood commercial corridors, and there are a lot of them: years ago the city's Commerce director put the count at around 265. Today the Department of Commerce still funds community groups to hire corridor managers and pays for corridor cleaning through its PHL Taking Care of Business program.

Each corridor has its own character, and that character is what a visitor searches for. A few examples:

CorridorWhat is thereWhat a site there should make clear
East Passyunk Avenue, South PhillyA business improvement district first designated in 2002, mostly locally owned shops and restaurants between Broad Street and Federal Street.Which block you are on, the nearest cross street and whether you take reservations or walk-ins.
Germantown AvenueA Belgian block avenue that ties Chestnut Hill, Mt. Airy and Germantown together, lined with restaurants, galleries and boutiques.Which neighborhood stretch you are in, because the avenue is long and the three feel different.
Main Street, ManayunkAbout 275 businesses, by Visit Philadelphia's count: shops, galleries, boutiques, bars and restaurants.Parking and hours, since weekend visitors decide on their phones before they come.

The same goes for Fishtown, Chinatown, Kensington and Northern Liberties. Customers name the neighborhood when they search, so your pages should too, along with the cross streets and the closest transit stop.

The license numbers a Philadelphia website should show

Philadelphia asks every person or company doing business in the city, including out-of-town businesses, to hold a Commercial Activity License. It costs nothing and is issued online through the city's eCLIPSE system. Trades carry more. Contractors who do construction, demolition or repair work need a city contractor license unless they work only on existing one- and two-family homes, and those home improvement contractors register with the Pennsylvania Attorney General's office instead. Plumbing, electrical and fire suppression work need a city trade license either way.

The city also says contractors must show their Contractor License Number on advertisements, stationery, proposals, job sites and company vehicles. Homeowners are told to check that a contractor is licensed before hiring. So the number is not just a rule to follow; it is a reason to trust you, and it should be easy to find.

  • Your contractor license or home improvement registration number in the footer of every page.
  • Your trade license type on the about page, in plain words: licensed plumber, licensed electrician.
  • The neighborhoods and suburbs you work in, so a homeowner knows you cover their block.
  • A quote form that asks for the address and the job, and emails it straight to you.

A new storefront deserves new photos online

The city's Storefront Improvement Program, run by the Department of Commerce, reimburses up to half the cost of exterior work for businesses and property owners on designated commercial corridors. As of June 2026 the cap is $20,000 for a single property and $30,000 for a corner or multi-address property, and the city says the program has now helped more than 1,000 businesses. Eligible work includes masonry, painting, windows, doors, lighting, signs and awnings, and the work has to be approved before it starts.

If you go through it, finish the job online too. The photos on your website and your Google Business Profile are often the first look a customer gets at your front door. A fresh facade with a five-year-old photo of the old one sends a mixed message. We build sites with a gallery and an about section that are easy to update when the scaffolding comes down.

Hiring one Philadelphia web designer instead of a firm

Many web designers in Philadelphia are part of a team. Dominion is one person: Maurice Johnson writes the pages, builds the site and answers your questions himself. That keeps the price fixed and the voice consistent, and it means projects that need a large team or custom software are not a fit, which we will say before you buy.

Keep the paperwork on your site current

Licenses get renewed, hours change, and a domain name expires if nobody watches the date. A site that still shows last year's license number or the old holiday hours costs trust quietly. Hosting, maintenance and updates are included while you keep the AI agent, or $49 a month without it, so changes like these are not a separate project.

On search, Google says local results turn on relevance, distance and prominence. Distance is fixed and prominence grows slowly. Relevance improves when your site and your Google Business Profile name your services, your corridor and your neighborhood clearly. Nobody can promise you a ranking, and we never do.

Free business help in Philadelphia

  • Office of Business ServicesPart of the city's Department of Commerce and the first stop for owners. A Business Services Manager helps work out which licenses and permits you need, with bilingual staff in Spanish, Mandarin and Korean.
  • Temple University SBDCNo-cost, confidential consulting for businesses in Philadelphia and Montgomery counties, plus free webinars on topics from digital marketing to building a website.
  • Pennsylvania SBDC networkThe statewide network's lead office moved from the Wharton School to Kutztown University in 2018, and Wharton's own SBDC center closed in 2019, so Philadelphia owners usually start with Temple.
  • Chamber of Commerce for Greater PhiladelphiaA regional business group whose members span eleven counties in three states.

Common questions

How do I find a good Philadelphia web designer?

Start with what you need the site to do, then ask each designer the same plain questions: what does it cost in total, who writes the words, who owns the domain and the finished site, and what happens if you stop paying monthly fees. Ask to see work built for a business like yours. Ours goes one step further: we build a free demo for your own business name, so you judge the actual site before you pay anything.

How much do web designers in Philadelphia charge?

Prices run from a few hundred dollars for a template setup to tens of thousands for an agency project, and many designers only quote after a call. Ours are printed. Starter is $497 for five hand-written pages, Pro is $997 for ten pages plus ten city pages, and Agency is $1,997 for research-led pages across your whole service area, all one time. Hosting, maintenance and updates are included while you keep the AI agent, or $49 a month without it. The AI agent itself is optional: the Pro chat widget is free for 14 days and the Agency phone agent for 7 days, then each is $297 a month.

Should my website show my Philadelphia license numbers?

For contractors, the city says your Contractor License Number belongs on your advertisements, proposals and company vehicles, and a website is the most visible advertising you have. Plumbers, electricians and fire suppression contractors also hold city trade licenses, and home improvement contractors register with the Pennsylvania Attorney General. We put the numbers you give us where customers can find them, usually the footer and the about page. Check the exact rule for your trade with Licenses and Inspections; we are not giving legal advice.

Can you build pages for the suburbs in Montgomery and Delaware counties?

Yes, for any town you actually serve. Pro includes ten city pages, each researched and written for that place, so a business in Northeast Philadelphia could add pages for the suburbs it drives to. Agency starts with keyword research across your whole area to decide which towns and services earn a page. We do not sell page counts; a few honest pages beat dozens of thin ones.

Will you meet with me in Philadelphia?

No. Dominion Web Design Pro is one person, Maurice Johnson, working from East Texas by phone, email and shared links. If an in-person meeting matters to you, the city has many local designers and you should hire one of them. If it does not, you get a free demo first and a phone line where an AI receptionist answers any hour and can transfer you to Maurice, the person writing your pages.

See your website before you pay for it

Give us your business name and what you do, and a demo site gets built for you to look at on your own phone. If you like it, pick a package. If you do not, you have spent nothing but the minute it took to look.
